narrativeBlocks.title: The scene
narrativeBlocks.body: Orestes has killed his mother to avenge his father. In Eumenides, Athena establishes a court to hear the conflict, and the pursuing Erinyes must also be addressed. The ending stages a negotiated civic settlement, not the disappearance of every competing claim.

narrativeBlocks.title: What the source does
narrativeBlocks.body: Source quotation (translation; whitespace normalized): “And I, returning from an exiled youth, Slew her, my mother—lo, it stands avowed! With blood for blood avenging my loved sire; And in this deed doth Loxias bear part, Decreeing agonies, to goad my will, Unless by me the guilty found their doom. Do thou decide if right or wrong were done— Thy dooming,”

narrativeBlocks.title: Why it matters
narrativeBlocks.body: Athena establishes a council-court for future cases. The Erinyes remain part of the settlement, so the play does not simply remove divine claims from justice.

narrativeBlocks.title: Read it carefully
narrativeBlocks.body: The trial does not simply remove the gods from justice. Athena and the Erinyes remain part of the settlement, so describe a change in the handling of claims rather than a clean replacement of religion by law.

narrativeBlocks.title: Carry it forward
narrativeBlocks.body: The heroic burden is being caught between irreconcilable duties.
